title: India and the US Expect a Trade Deal Within Weeks. The Tariff Threat Still Looms.
excerpt: A two-way agreement is on the table, but India wants a written guarantee: no future tariffs after the deal is signed. Washington has not yet agreed.
body:
A bilateral trade deal between India and the United States is expected to be finalised within weeks, according to an Indian trade official — but New Delhi is insisting on a condition Washington has not yet met: a written assurance that India will not be hit with additional tariffs after the agreement is signed.

The official, speaking on Monday, said the deal can be completed after the conclusion of the US Trade Representative's ongoing Section 301 investigation into India's trade practices. The probe, which examines whether India's policies constitute unfair barriers to American goods and services, has been one of the most contentious elements of the bilateral economic relationship under the Trump administration.

## The Tariff Guarantee India Wants

India's demand for a no-future-tariffs clause reflects hard-won experience. Over the past two years, Indian exports have faced a patchwork of American tariffs — from the broad reciprocal tariffs applied to most trading partners, to the more targeted Section 301 measures that could impose an additional 12% duty on Indian goods.

New Delhi's position is straightforward: if India makes concessions in a bilateral deal — lowering duties on American agricultural products, opening up its services market, easing regulatory barriers — it wants certainty that the US will not unilaterally impose new tariffs through executive action after the ink is dry.

That certainty has been elusive. The Trump administration has used tariff authority aggressively and unpredictably, sometimes reversing or escalating trade measures within weeks of announcing them.

## $220 Billion and Counting

The scale of the relationship gives both sides a strong incentive to close a deal. US Ambassador Atul Gor, speaking at a recent event, noted that bilateral trade in goods and services has skyrocketed from $20 billion to over $220 billion in the past two decades.

"We fully expect that the trade deal will be signed over the next few weeks and months," Gor said, adding that a high-level US trade delegation visited India from June 1 to 4 to work through the remaining clauses.

The ambassador framed the economic relationship in broader strategic terms. "The importance of India is now… not only economically but strategically to the world," he said — language that echoes the Biden-era Quad framework but with a transactional edge that is distinctly Trumpian.

## What's on the Table

While the specific terms of the deal have not been publicly disclosed, the broad contours have emerged from months of negotiation:

**Market access**: India is expected to lower tariffs on select American goods, particularly agricultural products such as almonds, apples, and dairy — sectors where American producers have long complained about prohibitive Indian duties.

**Services and digital trade**: The US is pushing for greater access for American technology and financial services companies, including relaxed data localisation requirements that have frustrated firms like Visa, Mastercard, and Amazon.

**Defence procurement**: India's growing defence imports from the US — which have risen from near zero to over $20 billion in the past decade — are likely to feature as a goodwill component, though they may not be formally part of the trade agreement.

**Intellectual property**: Pharmaceutical IP protections remain a sensitive area. India's generic drug industry, which supplies affordable medication to much of the developing world, has resisted US demands for stronger patent protections.

## The Section 301 Shadow

The USTR's Section 301 investigation is the elephant in the room. If the probe concludes that India's trade practices are unfair, it could trigger additional tariffs of up to 12% on Indian exports — on top of the existing tariff structure.

India's strategy appears to be completing a bilateral deal that renders the 301 findings moot, or at least politically inconvenient to act on. The logic: if the two countries sign a comprehensive trade agreement, slapping new tariffs afterward would undermine the deal before it has time to work.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For the estimated 4.4 million Indian Americans, a trade deal matters beyond the macroeconomic numbers. It affects the cost of goods shipped between the two countries — from Indian spices and textiles to American electronics and consumer brands. It shapes the regulatory environment for the tens of thousands of Indian-origin entrepreneurs who operate cross-border businesses.

And it signals whether the US-India relationship, which has been described by leaders on both sides as the "defining partnership of the 21st century," can translate rhetorical warmth into enforceable economic commitments. The next few weeks will tell.
